guidance.heading: OUTLOOK
section: The U.S.-Iran conflict continues to create uncertainty across crude oil and refined product markets. Middle Eastern crude exports recovered substantially toward the end of the third quarter, although ongoing threats to shipping and infrastructure, elevated freight and insurance costs, and low inventories continue to support higher prices and volatility. OPEC+ has paused further production increases during this crisis, but the pace of production and export recovery remains an important driver of global supply.

Refined product markets remain tight, with Middle Eastern fuel exports recovering more slowly than crude shipments. Low distillate inventories and refinery disruptions, including damage to Russian refineries, continue to support diesel prices. Refinery availability, seasonal maintenance and winter demand will influence market tightness, while additional strategic inventory releases could provide near-term relief. While U.S. policymakers considered diesel export restrictions during the quarter, no broad ban has been implemented.

In North America, higher Canadian supply and increased Venezuelan shipments alongside refinery outages impacting heavy crude conversion capacity are pressuring heavy crude differentials, compounded by elevated export shipping costs.

The price outlook remains dependent on geopolitical developments, the recovery of Middle Eastern supply and inventory replenishment. Further disruptions could increase prices, while sustained export recovery or weaker economic activity could reduce supply risk premiums and limit price increases.
In addition to the above, our commodity pricing outlook for the next 12 months is influenced by the following:
•OPEC+ policy and the pace at which Middle East producers are able to bring back curtailed supply.
•In the near-term, there is a higher risk of a tariff-induced global economic slowdown that could slow oil demand.

•We expect the WTI-WCS at Hardisty differential will remain largely tied to global supply factors, including incremental Venezuelan imports into the USGC and heavy crude oil processing capacity, as long as supply does not exceed Canadian crude oil export capacity.
•Refined product prices and market crack spreads are likely to continue to fluctuate, adjusting for seasonal trends and refinery utilization in North America and globally.
•RINs prices will continue to be impacted by future policy decisions including Small Refinery Exemption waivers, reallocation of exempted volumes and policies around imported biofuel RINs generation.

desk.headline: Revenue up 21% to C$16.0bn and EPS of C$1.83 vs C$0.72 on record 1m+ BOE/d output; no change to guidance stated in release

numbers.eps_basis: diluted GAAP (IFRS net earnings per share)

results: Revenue rose 21% to C$16.0bn and net earnings to C$3.4bn (C$1.83 a share) from C$1.3bn, on higher oil prices, record Oil Sands output and strong refining margins.
Upstream production passed 1m BOE a day for the first time (1,024 MBOE/d, +23% y/y), helped by the MEG acquisition and records at Foster Creek, Christina Lake and Sunrise.
Downstream operating margin jumped to C$1.8bn from C$0.4bn a year ago despite the Lima refinery turnaround; US refining market capture was 88%, helped by small-refinery waivers.
Free funds flow was C$3.6bn; C$1.9bn went back to shareholders (C$1.5bn buybacks, C$403m dividends) and net debt fell to C$3.0bn.
Cenovus agreed in October to buy Athabasca Oil (about C$5.7bn enterprise value), adding about 45 MBOE/d; closing is expected in December.

guidance.summary: The release gives no new production or spending ranges and does not say whether full-year guidance changed; it points to updated 2026 guidance on the company website, which we could not check. It flags a Q4 hit from US refinery maintenance and a commodity outlook driven by the US-Iran conflict.
